name: Coaches experience
criteria: Clubs are required to list the coaching background, history, and number of years of the current valid qualifications for all academy coaches and academy goalkeeping coaches. This may also include relevant past experiences and/or significant relevant tertiary education. Coaches operating across multiple age groups will be scored per age group. Age groups where there are boys' and girls' coaches identified with an asterisk (i.e., u11 Boys coach and u11 Girls coach, u18 Boys coach and u18 Girls coach, etc.) will take an average score across the two programs. Technical Lead positions do not score in this area.

name: Technical Leads (PT / FT)
criteria: Technical Lead staff will also be scored based on whether they are Full Time or Part Time within the club’s program. Clubs will be rewarded for employing a higher number of Full Time Technical Leads. Position Descriptions must be uploaded as part of the club’s NN07 submission to receive points in this area.

name: Club Values, Mission, Vision and Philosophy
criteria:
The club's values, mission, vision, and philosophy are clearly articulated, with a high level of detail and explanation regarding how they are implemented throughout the club.

The club’s values are clearly articulated and explained in detail, outlining their meaning and purpose. They are directly connected to the club’s player development processes and are supported through evidence in planning and delivery documentation. They align with the local football community and are reflected in the club's member’s behaviours.

The club's mission encompasses its role within the community and its service to members. It appropriately aligns its current service delivery with its place in the football ecosystem while demonstrating potential for future growth and development.

The club’s vision provides a clear pathway for future progress, supported by a multi-year plan that details technical, operational, and financial goals. The vision demonstrates strategic foresight, highlighting opportunities for innovation and adaptability to the evolving football landscape.

The club's philosophy appropriately represents its members, community, and historical background. It aims to promote a clear set of guiding principles and beliefs that will influence future behaviours. The philosophy should also include information that establishes a solid foundation to ensure that player development remains the primary focus (for the club and the wider academy). It encourages innovation, enabling goal setting and the creation of pathways to success.

The overall content of the values, mission, vision, and philosophy, from a technical perspective, reflects the growth of the game and the club, with departmental growth supported by a multidisciplinary approach.

name: Player Development and Coaching Methodology Principles
criteria:
The P2 document, which provides the complete framework for player development at the club, should be logically structured, easy to navigate, and designed to be a practical day-to-day resource that guides coaching staff in the consistent delivery of the club's player development philosophy and methodology.

The club’s philosophy, methodology, and principles on how player development is implemented throughout the academy should be clearly articulated to ensure the best possible chance of achieving positive player development outcomes. This methodology should guide the complete implementation of program delivery and support the values, mission, vision, and philosophy of the club.

The methodology should prioritise individual player development, detailing how this will be achieved across all development phases of the academy. The club needs to outline its Long-Term Athlete Development (LTAD) framework, which should align with an evidence-based, holistic approach. This framework should account for individual differences while providing a common roadmap to success. The program’s goals should be appropriately matched to the players’ age and stage of learning and development, encompassing the physical, technical-tactical, psychological, and social aspects of player growth.

The club provides a detailed breakdown of its age-specific coaching content, outlining how each age, stage, and phase are catered for in alignment with long-term player development. Detailed coaching content and principles are clearly articulated for each age group and development phase to reflect the overall player development methodology. A breakdown of the session framework for each age and phase should be included within the age-specific guidelines to ensures alignment with the coaching content and principles.

The club is encouraged to articulates how they intend to link their unique methodology and philosophy with the 'Future Queensland Player' Framework, with detail around how they intend to develop these qualities particularly within the U9-U15 age groups.

The club’s coaching methodology should follow an evidence-based approach to teaching and learning, incorporating preferred coaching principles for the relevant ages and stages of delivery. This should include a variety of training and game day contexts. The coaching principles are clearly communicated, with specific guidance on how and when they should be implemented and delivered. The methodology should support a holistic approach to player development and be reinforced through coach education, model sessions, and regular consultation led by the Technical Director, technical staff, or industry experts. There should be clear evidence of coach buy-in and shared understanding across the club regarding the player development and coaching methodology.

name: Club Based Playing Style
criteria:
The Club Based Playing Style is an extremely important document in place to support the club's player development framework outlined in the P2 document.

The Club Based Playing Style is based on clear principles applied throughout the main moments of the game and informs the players about their roles in a dynamic context. The model is intentionally designed to prioritise development outcomes for all players over immediate results. All club coaches work in alignment with this model, which is tailored to suit the ages and stages it is implemented in. In the junior development phase, the playing style should be based more on key technical behaviours, rather than team principles. The playing style encourages the development of creative and adaptable players, focusing less on formations or systems and more on behaviours and relationships within units.

The club must define how its unique Playing Style should be brought to life, with specific articulation for each relevant age and stage. Additionally, the club should provide detailed guidance on how the principles aligns with the player development pathway.

A logical and methodical process is applied when conveying the model across the development phases. The playing style is designed to cultivate the fundamental characteristics of the type of player the club aims to produce, ensuring consistency without contradictions. This playing style is well-understood throughout the club and is evident in the planning and delivery of all sessions—whether for teams, units, or individual players.

While the playing style remains unique to each club, the club is encouraged to outline how the documentation aligns with the 'Future Queensland Player' framework, with reference to how the playing style will support this framework.

Technical directors and technical leads not only articulate and explain the team model but also evaluate its implementation and assess the progress of coaches and teams in applying it. There is a high level of club-wide understanding regarding the delivery of the team model across all age groups.

In the delivery component of the assessment, clubs will be assessed on how consistently the playing style is implemented across all ages and phases.

name: Individual Development Planning Guidelines
criteria:
There is a clear strategy and club philosophy, supported by a high level of club-wide understanding regarding the planning and implementation of individual development guidelines. The planning clearly outlines specialised windows for individualised training, which are consistently integrated into team training sessions or specifically delivered in small group/specialised sessions by specialist coaches as appropriate. These planned sessions align with best practice models and are supported by concurrent information and progress assessments. The individual development guidelines should also outline how these principles are applied and demonstrated on match days.

There are feedback procedures in place to appraise overall progress and each player’s development. These may include instructions on initial evaluation, goal setting, and the approach to be taken (e.g., improvement or mastery-based, self-guided, etc.). There is a well-articulated management system in place at the club to monitor individual player development (e.g. Player IDPs) and its planning. This system demonstrates that individual development is at the core of their delivery, consistently evidenced in club training and match day environments.

The club ensures that there is a good understanding across all staff what the guidelines mean in terms of practical delivery with clearly defined responsibilities for planning, monitoring, and reviewing player development. There is evidence of data used where possible across multiple occasions throughout the season to quantify individual player development. Consideration is made to ensure that guidelines are followed uniformly across the club and in the correct manner.

name: Goalkeeper Development Strategy
criteria:
The club has a clear long-term vision and strategy for the development of goalkeepers. The goalkeeping development strategy establishes a unique set of goalkeeper principles, periodic training cycles, and a session library that align with and complement the overall team model, playing style, and values of the club. Within the club's playing style, the goalkeeper's technical and tactical roles and responsibilities are clearly defined and aligned through each development phase.

The strategy articulates the technical-tactical, psychosocial, and physical expectations specific to each development stage and phase, with a particular focus on the competencies the goalkeeper should possess at various stages of development. There is a clear alignment with development and age-specific methodology and pedagogy to support the goalkeeper’s long-term development.

The strategy outlines a clear process for providing ongoing feedback from the goalkeeping department on training and match-day performance, linking this feedback to the goalkeeper’s individual development plan and evaluations.

The club clearly articulates its goalkeeping development plan to key stakeholders (players, parents, goalkeeping and other coaching staff) to create a shared understanding of the importance and objectives of the Goalkeeping Development Strategy. More emphasis should be placed on club-based goalkeeping coaches delivering upon this planning. Any external providers should adhere to the club’s ethos and coaching methodology.

name: Annual Season Plan and Training Schedule
criteria:
An annual calendar is provided for all age groups, bringing together all key activities and creating synergies by keeping stakeholders on track with deadlines for each activity. The annual calendar spans a minimum of 40 weeks and outlines pre-season, physical testing, training cycles, match dates, inductions, player education workshops, player reviews, season debriefings, and other coordinated meetings with players, parents, and coaching staff across all age groups in their programs. This holistic approach ensures a connection between activities, with logical steps followed in a cyclical manner.

The club needs to demonstrate how it uses this document to plan wider activities and events across the club. Additionally, the club maintains a documented training schedule that outlines session times and locations for all teams, including specialist units, individual sessions, and goalkeeper training. The training times are structured to maximise staffing and the availability of the Technical Directors or Technical Leads, while also considering the availability of training fields.

The training system may include physical training (gym, strength and conditioning, movement competencies, etc.), meeting times or placeholders for video analysis, match reviews, and tactical, physical, psychological, or wellbeing education workshops. It is the club’s responsibility to ensure the schedule is updated weekly, as the execution of this plan can be observed during FQ club visits.

name: Principles of Periodisation and Training Program Cycles
criteria:
The club’s approach to periodisation aligns with recognised evidence-based practice, ensuring consistent cycle lengths and clear links to the club’s Youth Development Plan. It integrates tactical periodisation, football conditioning, and workload tracking to promote holistic player development across tactical, technical, physical, psychological, and social areas.

Training cycles are appropriately differentiated for each age and stage, with progressive loading applied to older age groups. A live, centralised library of training program cycles is maintained and accessible to all relevant technical staff.

Each training cycle demonstrates clear links between training and match day objectives, with the plan regularly reviewed and updated to remain current and observable within the daily environment.

The delivery of these topics can be observed during FQ club visits or referenced in the Technical Director and Technical Lead’s evaluation of coaches, teams, or individual development progress.

name: Talent Development Philosophy
criteria:
The club's beliefs focus on identifying and nurturing talent. The planning in this area should reflect how individual talent is recognised and developed through the training environment created at the club. The club’s philosophy prioritises promoting the best interests of each individual and providing opportunities for them to progress to state and national levels. The club collaborates with FQ Academy, QST, QAS, and A-League Academies.

The club has a detailed statement regarding talent management, which includes several best practice elements. The core of their talent management is based on an individualised approach. The club understands its role within the local community, supports players from the region, and ensures they have opportunities to engage with the club. The intent is not to hold 'open trials' but to follow a long-term approach to player development. The club’s talent identification processes assess the potential of players rather than focusing solely on current performance. The technical staff are aware of growth and maturation factors, and their talent identification decisions are based on a holistic approach (e.g., FA's technical skills and player competencies), in alignment with the club's vision and philosophy.

The talent management philosophy emphasises that master coaching is a key factor, and talent development is considered a ‘whole-of-club’ responsibility. The club prioritises patience with junior players and avoids early deselection. Appropriate succession planning ensures that there is sufficient identification of talent within or outside the club for u9-u18 players. It should be noted that this may be assessed during interviews and club visits to determine whether the philosophy is not only documented but also supported by a high level of club-wide understanding across all staff.

name: Talent ID Policy and Player Profiles
criteria:
The club has a clearly defined Talent ID Policy that articulates how, when, and why newly identified players are recruited, or existing talents are retained or released. The Policy acknowledges its focus on long-term athlete development, which potentially results in consistently high retention rates and multi-year offers. A recruitment process is in place to identify and assess whether players are suitable for the club. This process details the roles and responsibilities of staff members and how they are utilised.

The club demonstrates how its policies and protocols for talent identification and progression best suit its environment. It demonstrates well-established connections and pathways within the community, including trusted sources such as schools, churches, clinics, and Memorandum of Understanding with local clubs and to the potential progression of players to FQ Development Programs. The network presented is integrated, and there is a planned approach to scouting players. Players may trial "in-season" with the approval of their current club and on an invitation-only basis.

The players' evaluation process is as objective as possible, with qualitative data collected and collated. Decisions are not based solely on a single coach’s opinion. Instead, a panel led by the Technical Director or Technical Lead spearheads the process, ensuring that Talent ID reflects the club’s player profiles.

The club strives to develop players in alignment with its vision and philosophy. Player profiles are specific to each developmental stage, with a focus on the competencies players should display and execute at each age and phase. These profiles may be used to assess players during the Talent ID process and as they transition through developmental stages. Player profiles include specific, position-related, or unit-based milestones. Ideally, there is a consistent link between Talent ID, player profiles, the playing style, and individual development at the club. Player profiles may also serve as a tool for internal assessments or reviews of the efficiency of the training process and policies.

name: Player Parent Induction Process
criteria:
The Player/ Parent Induction process is thorough and details all the required content that will be essential for the season including operational, technical, medical, child protection and complaint resolution procedures. The induction covers all age groups between u9 to u18 and may be delivered separately for different age groups. Inductions should be completed before the season's start with content, exact date(s) and groups attended evidenced. The club must submit the presented slides that was shared at the event to prove there is comprehensive communication.

Lines of communication, grievance

whistleblowing processes are communicated along with child protection and serious complaints procedure. The communication process sets out protection for players, parents and coaches in terms of how and when dialogue is appropriate. The club’s player welfare officer is introduced and made available. Codes of conduct are detailed; expectations are specified to create a safe environment with responsible actions.

Attendance, game time and game start keeping policies are articulated. Players’ medical screening is ideally completed by that time and follow up plans for prehab/conditioning programs for pre-season are accessible (while similar services for competition and post-season phases are outlined). Injured players understand in-season medical support and return to play protocols.

The club might provide an overview of their mission, vision, philosophy in player development, high level details of the coaching methodology, the program’s individual player focus and playing style. Players are completely comfortable in the organisation for their season; they know where to be and when and are provided with information about the equipment they will receive or need to source.

name: Goal Setting and Individual Development Plans
criteria:
Goal Setting and Individual Development Plans (IDPs) reflect the club’s commitment to engaging players in a structured, ongoing process of setting, reviewing, and refining their development goals. The club clearly articulates how, why, and when goals are set, ensuring all players and coaches understand the process and their shared responsibilities within it.

Regularly planned review meetings form a key part of each player’s development journey, allowing for collaborative discussions between players, coaches, and specialist staff. Players have meaningful input into their goals and are regularly reminded of them through a consistent, process-driven framework.

The framework supports the creation of S.M.A.R.T. goals that focus on mastery, effort, and continual improvement. Technical Directors, coaches, and specialist staff may ‘screen’ or validate goals to ensure they are realistic and developmentally appropriate. Goals are integrated within each player’s Individual Development Plan, linking directly to the club’s broader player development philosophy and methodology.

Each IDP may include goals across technical, tactical, physical, and psychological domains, with evidence of regular updates and ongoing monitoring. The framework incorporates defined checkpoints and follow-up protocols to support player reflection and progress.

To enhance engagement and clarity, IDPs are supported with video footage aligned to each player’s goals and strengths, with players encouraged to contribute or identify clips themselves. Overall, the club demonstrates through its documentation and practice a clear, well-developed strategy for developing individuals within its program.

name: Athlete Welfare and Support
criteria:
This area assesses the club’s planned and professionally delivered welfare and wellbeing support for players, and how this framework is embedded across the club environment.

The club provides detailed and thorough evidence of how, when, and by whom players are supported throughout their journey at the club. Welfare strategies are proactive, evidence-based, and reflect the individual and collective needs of athletes, with processes in place to monitor and measure their effectiveness.

The club maintains a comprehensive Child Protection Policy, understood and signed off by all staff and volunteers, and appoints a qualified Club Welfare Officer with a clear position description, relevant qualifications and/or Blue Card, and a direct communication process to recognised safeguarding authorities. Members are informed of the Welfare Officer’s role, contact details, and the support services available.

Athlete welfare and wellbeing strategies are holistic and follow a bio-psycho-social philosophy, recognising the interconnection between physical, psychological, social, cultural, and environmental factors. The club actively provides support in at least three of these key wellbeing dimensions, demonstrating an environment that values balanced development both on and off the field.

A formal mental health referral process is in place to ensure members can access best-practice information, advice, and services. The club also appoints a School Liaison Officer with a defined role description and demonstrates commitment to players’ academic and personal growth through at least two structured initiatives, such as school MOUs, homework or study provisions, or coordinated transport support.

name: Sport Science Support
criteria:
The Club has a clear philosophy to support and nurture talent at the club. Areas such as nutrition, physical testing, athletic development, injury prevention, recovery, hydration, Talent ID, maturation and growth, health and wellbeing, and education are all appropriately and carefully planned to align with age specific milestones and development.

The club has a fully integrated High-Performance department that is appropriately qualified to monitor and assess players in its care.

The high-performance department has full reporting lines to physio, strength and conditioning staff (rehab/prehab/performance development), technical staff, and other relevant parties.

Beyond the guiding philosophy, the club implements a comprehensive and periodised annual plan for the physical development of players. This plan integrates both on-field and off-field strength and conditioning components, aligns with age and maturation stages, and demonstrates a consistent and evidence-based approach to monitoring and adjusting player workloads throughout the season.

The assessment of this area covers the personnel employed by the club, and it will be assessed if the High-Performance department influence practices in player development to help keep up with modern trends.

name: Club Coach Development Strategy
criteria:
The club has a clear and well-defined coach development strategy to support the professional and personal growth of its coaches. This is demonstrated by a high level of strategic planning and a significant number of annual educational events hosted at the club, providing an informal education process for all coaches from U9s to U18s.

The strategy outlines a detailed profile for each member of the coaching staff as part of their individual development plan, highlighting their key strengths, main areas for development, and a tailored plan to support their progression toward formal qualifications in the short, medium, and long term, either internally within the club or externally within the Football Queensland programs that are designed to advance identified coaches. Additionally, the plan informs the club’s management about the Technical Director’s and Technical Lead’s responsibilities, tasks, and performance in relation to coach development.

Key components of the plan may include the club's optimal/ideal coach profile, recruitment strategies for coaching talent, availability of mentoring opportunities, both informal and formal educational events, individual development plans (IDPs), self-reflection protocols, and access to bursaries or scholarship. It may also allocate time for coaches to explore areas of development beyond technical coaching, such as sports science, sports psychology, match analysis, talent identification, or other relevant disciplines. The strategy ensures that all staff have access to these opportunities, which may span various disciplines within the club.

The strategy should include mid- and long-term goals from the club’s perspective, along with a clear plan on how the Club intend to achieve 50/50 gender parity in coaching positions.

name: Coach Onboarding and Retention Process
criteria:
The club has a clear and detailed process for onboarding and retention of coaches, both new and retained, across all age groups from u9s to u18s. Coaches are provided with a structured onboarding process that extends beyond an 'induction night' event/s and adequately prepares them before they begin their coaching responsibilities. As part of this process, clubs could hold mid-year and end-of-season meetings with coaches to discuss performance reviews and development opportunities.

From an HR perspective, coaches are welcomed with a thorough explanation of all policies and procedures. These include member protection protocols such as blue cards protocol, safeguarding protocols, complaints processes, and more. They are introduced to key figures within the club, including the president, board members, general manager, technical directors and technical leads, other coaches, staff members, players, and parents, etc. From a technical standpoint, coaches are provided with a comprehensive overview of the club’s Player Development and Coaching Methodology Principles (and other key documentation), which align with its overarching values, mission, vision and philosophy at the Club.

Where applicable, clubs provide evidence that coaches are given a detailed position description and/or a formal contract or agreement. These may include key performance indicators (KPIs) to clarify their roles and responsibilities. They may serve a probationary period during which they receive ongoing feedback and support from the Technical Directors and Technical Leads. Coaches are expected to become familiar with the club's football operations and, where possible, receive a full briefing on the team and players they will work with. This includes reviewing previous reports, accessing the players' most current development plans, and receiving updates on relevant matters such as personality traits, injuries, family circumstances, or other pertinent information. By the end of the induction process, all staff members must be well-versed in the coaching methodology, playing style, player feedback and review processes, as well as deadlines and record-keeping protocols. Coaches are also informed about how their performance will be assessed and reviewed, and the development and support opportunities available to them.

The club provides evidence of an effective system for tracking the coach onboarding and retention process throughout the season, which includes documenting the date, time, and location of sessions and meetings, staff members in attendance, the content covered during the induction, and any other relevant details.

name: Attendance and Game Time Record
criteria:
Provide attendance and game time records to date for all relevant age groups. These records help identify trends in player attendance and game time and enable the club to trigger appropriate follow-up actions or support for players. They can also be used as part of the player review process.

The club has a well-planned method for attendance recording, and the data process allows coaches and technicians easy access to relevant information. Attendance records include reasons for absence, which may trigger follow-up actions. Logs are kept up to date and accessible for the Technical Director or Technical Lead to resolve issues relating to game time, player selection, or adherence to club policies. Attendance data may also link to player welfare tracking, supporting early identification of social or psychological concerns.

The club maintains a detailed process for logging player game time. Coaches and the Technical Director or Technical Lead can access this information freely, and it is updated weekly. Game time data provides insights that inform decisions on player development, squad placement, playing minutes, and positional exposure, and can be integrated into player reports and development plans.

Game time data is reviewed against the planned framework for each age group to ensure alignment with the club’s development approach. The information is used to check conformity to planned targets and inform future planning, including arranging additional matches or friendlies where required.

name: Workload Tracking
criteria:
Provide workload records to date for all age-appropriate groups. These records are used by coaches and S&C staff to understand player development, prevent overload or underload, and optimise training and match stimulus.

The club has an integrated system for tracking player workloads across all daily physical activities (club, school, and other sports). The system is easily accessible to staff, and players are kept informed through dashboards, noticeboards, or other appropriate methods.

Workload data is captured through appropriate measures such as Relative Perceived Exertion (RPE) and, at older age groups, GPS data. The club’s sports scientist oversees data collection and can generate daily or weekly reports for technical staff to inform future training design. This system is used across the academy, not limited to the first team.

Coaches receive education on interpreting and applying workload data, integrating it into their planning routines. Team loading targets are structured in micro- and meso-cycles, with data used to compare planned versus actual physical output. Individual top-up or pull-back adjustments are made where required.

Workload tracking also supports the medical team in return-to-play processes and monitoring overuse injury trends. It may be coupled with wellbeing monitoring to adopt a holistic approach. Player self-reporting contributes to feedback processes and demonstrates responsibility for managing their own bodies.

name: Wellbeing Monitoring
criteria:
Provide wellbeing records to date for all age-appropriate groups. These records help coaches ensure that all players under their care are supported and provide a clear red-flag system to identify athletes requiring attention.

A qualified Club Wellbeing Officer oversees this process, supported by medical and technical staff (Physio, Psychologist, Doctor, Club Liaison, Technical Lead and Technical Director). The officer manages documentation, follow-up, and coordination between the club and external contacts such as schools or relevant authorities when serious issues arise. The role has a clear position description, formal support from the board, and access to all player contact details.

Players have access to a wellbeing monitoring platform that can be used remotely and in which they have confidence regarding the red-flag process and data privacy. All relevant staff have access to this information to inform player care and adapt training expectations accordingly.

Beyond monitoring, the club provides education sessions and wellbeing programs for players and parents that address physical, social, psychological, and environmental wellbeing, supporting a proactive and preventative culture.

name: Sport Science Monitoring, Support & Athletic Development
criteria:
Provide maturation data (Bio-Banding, Peak Height Velocity (PHV), etc.) and relevant physical testing records to date for all age-appropriate groups. Clubs are assessed on their ability to accurately record players’ physiological maturation and age-appropriate physical performance data, and demonstrate how this information informs training prescription, athletic development programming, team placement, player assessment, Talent ID, and player welfare.

Clubs achieve higher scores when all key maturation monitoring methodologies (minimum six times per year) and physical performance assessments (minimum three times per year) are conducted and recorded regularly across all relevant teams. High-scoring clubs analyse this data through sport science staff and ensure findings are effectively communicated to coaching staff to enhance player development practices and technical decision-making. This should include classifying players according to their rate of development (e.g. early, average, or late developers).

Physical testing should be age-appropriate and used to establish player benchmarks, monitor physical development over time, identify individual needs, and inform individualised exercise prescription throughout both pre-season and in-season.

These records should support individual player development, guide the management of players through key stages of maturation, and safeguard late developers and players experiencing their PHV growth-spurt phase.

name: Return To Play Process
criteria:
Provide records and proof of process to date for each age group. These records demonstrate that the club has an individualised return-to-play process to support injured players back into training and match play.

Evidence should include documentation from a qualified physiotherapist who collaborates with high-performance staff to minimise the risk of injury or re-injury through a clear, progressive return-to-training plan provided to coaches.

The club maintains fully integrated communication between the physiotherapist or doctor, sports scientist/S&C coach, and technical department. Each discipline recognises its role within the process and contributes to the player’s safe return to full fitness. All stakeholders access a single, secure reference system that stores player injury records, availability status, and relevant medical notes (with appropriate permission levels). Player injury histories are retained for several years, including post-departure, to satisfy insurance and player-transfer requirements.

The return-to-play process is informed by historical data and strengthened by prevention measures such as pre-season screening and personalised prehabilitation programs targeting strength or balance discrepancies. The club also maintains clear policies and procedures for concussion management, emergency response (defibrillator, EpiPen), and serious-injury protocols. Baseline fitness and concussion tests are completed at the start of each season or when new players join. Where possible, the club works with a preferred doctor or surgeon to support serious-injury management and establish best practice standards.

name: Session Plan Library
criteria:
The club’s session plan library is stored in a centralised, easily accessible location for all coaching staff and is available to FQ Club Development Ambassadors prior to club visits. Session plans for all age groups are player-specific, current, and reviewed by the Technical Director to ensure a consistent approach across the program.

Coaches can access session plans from other age groups to encourage collaboration and knowledge sharing. All session plans align with the club’s periodisation framework and reflect its player development and coaching methodology principles.

Session plans, including goalkeeper, individualised, and specialised sessions, are clearly evidenced and uploaded using a consistent naming convention across all ages and stages. Additional planning evidence may also be provided where relevant.

name: Video Analysis Services
criteria:
The club possesses adequate equipment for filming matches and operates an associated video analysis platform that supports player and team development. There is clear evidence of consistent match-day footage being recorded for all teams throughout the season (ideally weekly, but at minimum fortnightly), with footage made available to all key stakeholders including players, coaches, parents, and medical staff.

An up-to-date video library is maintained, reflecting the club’s playing style and key individual techniques. This library serves as evidence of the club’s methodology and is accessible to stakeholders as part of the club’s learning environment. Match footage is actively used by an analyst or team coaches to create individual and team development clips, such as match reviews, opposition analysis, and unit feedback sessions.

Players regularly receive individual clips or have access to systems where they can self-identify and share their own clips with relevant staff. There is a structured feedback process in place within the club that supports player development through review presentations, one-to-one discussions, or the use of AI-driven platforms providing key highlights and performance statistics. The process is coordinated by a dedicated analyst (this can be as part of a dual role) who works closely with coaches and players to maximise the use of video evidence and ensure feedback is objective, consistent, and developmentally focused.

name: Training Delivery Observation
criteria:
No submission required. Training sessions are observed to assess how effectively the club’s player development and coaching methodology are delivered. There is clear evidence of a structured training plan with consistent delivery across groups within each development phase. Session areas are organised to promote connection between players and coaches and to allow effective monitoring.

A Technical Lead oversees sessions, providing direction, support, and feedback where required, within a recognisable and inclusive culture that reflects the club’s values. Technical detail is evident throughout delivery, and coaches demonstrate a strong understanding of the session content, methodology, and intended outcomes. Each session has clear technical and/or tactical objectives linked to the training cycle and tailored to individual or team needs.

Preparation and organisation are timely; field space, equipment, and staffing are used efficiently. Coaches manage time and flow between components effectively, adapting practices to meet player or team needs. Interventions show high levels of football knowledge and observation skills. Feedback is timely, relevant, and age-appropriate, supporting meaningful player learning.

Sessions conclude with evaluation and reflection that involve players and staff in reviewing delivery and learning outcomes. The appearance, behaviour, and overall conduct of coaches align with the club’s values and beliefs.

The club should provide pre-visit access to its session library and training schedule, ensuring planned sessions align with training cycles and are stored electronically to support collaboration and shared learning. All academy coaches adhere to the detailed methodology and intervention standards established by the club.

Full marks are awarded when there is clear consistency and alignment between the boys' and girls' programs, in the delivery of the club's player development philosophy, coaching methodology, and delivery standards.

name: Coach Interaction Observation (Training)
criteria:
No submission required. It will be observed during club visits when the coaches interact with players, coaching staff and other club staff members. This area looks to assess the interactions of coaches before, during and after training sessions and team meetings. This evaluation is also about the human side of coaching and leadership that goes beyond the technicalities; from the start of the session to the close, how coaches set up the environment and how coaches generally affect player behaviours and actions.

The following essential traits for successful coaching interactions are to be observed at training or team meetings:

1.) Clear, concise, and effective communication to deliver key messages,

2.) Ability to ask purposeful questions, engage and guide players,

3.) Appropriate mannerisms, tone and body language,

4.) Skill to find the balance when to motivate, influence and inspire,

5.) Ability to create a learning environment where players are engaged and included,

6.) Positive interactions with team members and club technical staff to exchange ideas, share knowledge or ask advice.

Full marks are awarded if there is clear consistency and alignment between the boys' and girls' programs in the delivery of the club's player development philosophy, coaching methodology, and delivery standards. The above interactions from the coach must be relevant to the age and stage of the player.

name: TD/TL Interaction Observation (Training)
criteria:
Technical Director (TD) and Technical Lead (TL) interaction observations will be assessed mainly during club visits. The Technical Director is the guardian of the club's coaching philosophy and methodology and actively interacts with and supports the club's technical staff in person. Where a Technical Lead is appointed, this role works in alignment with and as an extension of the Technical Director, ensuring consistency of message, methodology, and standards across all age phases.

The foundation of a positive and engaging TD/TL interaction in the club environment are:

1.) 1 on 1 meeting and mentoring of coaches.

2.) Workshops for coaches and regular in person meetings.

3.) Training observations with formal or informal feedback.

4.) Model sessions or best practice observations of external presenters.

During these occasions the TD/TL displays:

A.) Outstanding football knowledge with the intent to share and to create a learning environment.

B.) The ability to care about coaches, players, staff.

C.) The ability to ask questions, engage and guide coaches and technical staff.

D.) The ability to effectively communicate with all key stakeholders.

The TD should retain the same level of influence and understanding across all areas of the program, ensuring consistent care, connection, and communication. All interactions from the TD/TL must be age and stage appropriate and demonstrate leadership, connection, and alignment with the club’s technical direction.

Full marks are awarded if there is clear consistency and alignment between the boys' and girls' programs in the resource allocation and delivery of the club's player development philosophy, coaching methodology, and delivery standards.

name: Individualised and Specialised Training
criteria:
Players gain development opportunities through training that is structured to assist them in meeting targets identified within their individual development plans (IDPs). Individual/specialised trainings are planned and offered as the core of the academy program. Training practices are designed to include specific contexts/techniques for individuals. Those trainings are regular and either built into the team training, held outside of those sessions, or replace team training from time to time. The key is regularity and specificity when attention is given to players individual improvement

mastery of skill or positional knowledge. The individual trainings are not ad-hoc or generic, they reflect on players needs since they follow specific and documented feedback from evaluation procedures.

The most advanced academy programs can allocate technical staff within the program to conduct specialised sessions and monitor individual player progress. The dates, content of individual/specialised training are recorded and documented, and they are regularly delivered as part of the training program. They are indicated in the annual plan and within training cycles as well. The athlete’s improvement is monitored, and the aim and progress of the program is clearly communicated to the players and parents.

Goalkeeper training is assessed separately and not included in this line item.

Full marks are awarded if the club demonstrates clear consistency, care and attention in the allocation of resources and delivery standards for both male and female players, ensuring equitable access to individualised and specialised training.

name: Female Player Development in Mixed Training and Playing Environments
criteria:
Female player development in a mixed environment is an effective solution to provide the best possible challenge for the most talented girls at FQ Academy clubs.

Clubs are required to have a documented structure that allows talented girls to train or play, either regularly or permanently, with boys in the Junior and Youth phases. It is expected that the Club’s Technical Director identifies female players who can benefit from training or playing with boys, creates a periodised plan to provide this challenge, informs the Club Development Ambassador, and connects with FQ’s Female Player Development Leads to consult with both about the best possible way to execute the plan. This collaboration should result in regular updates, the sharing of players’ Individual Development Plans, and preparing the players to participate in FQ Emerging or Queensland State Team training in the future.

The club may also offer merged training sessions or in-house mixed games between teams through evidenced and documented planning. Lastly, a club’s commitment to contributing to the creation of a mixed football environment will also be positively recognised if the club fields competitive boys’ teams in friendly matches against the girls’ Queensland State Team or QAS program.

Playing opportunities for female players in boys’ competitions during the Youth phase may require formal approval. Granting this opportunity remains at Football Queensland’s sole discretion, based on the Technical Department’s advice and in line with the Rules of Competition applied by the FQ Competitions Department.

name: Goalkeeping Development Delivery
criteria:
No submission required. The club provides appropriate field space to conduct all forms of goalkeeping practice, including crossing, distribution, and game-realistic situations. Goalkeeping sessions are well organised and structured to meet both individual and group needs, demonstrating excellent planning and organisation from the coach. Practices show a strong balance between execution-based and game-related elements that are age- and stage-appropriate, aligned to a clear session objective or topic.

The goalkeeping coach displays a thorough understanding of goalkeeping techniques and positional roles within the game, communicating key concepts clearly and effectively. The coach’s intervention process is clear, concise, and consistent, utilising modelling and demonstrations to support player understanding.

There is clear evidence that the goalkeeping coach attends a high proportion of match days to provide both formal and informal feedback to goalkeepers across the junior and youth academy phases, ensuring individual progression and alignment with the club’s overall player development methodology.

The club is encouraged to provide access pre-visit to the club’s session library and training schedule and planned training sessions are in line with cycles.

name: Medical Standards
criteria:
The club has a medical room on site with first aid equipment, ice and strapping supply (free of charge for players), stretcher and defibrillator.  At minimum, a Level 1 Sports Trainer is available on training nights and games to provide strapping and first aid and a physio for triage and match days. The club's physio or a preferred physio practice is the point of contact for players who require ongoing treatment, preferably at a discounted rate.

Assessment is not solely concerned with sports trainer or physio cover of games and sessions, but the club should demonstrate how the full coverage of players health is delivered throughout the season. Assessment will also look at the records that are kept by the club and how the club ensures that there are measures in place to detail the training and medical history of any player at the club.

name: Adherence to Club's Player Development Philosophy and Playing Style
criteria:
Adherence to the club’s playing style is observed during match visits or via access to the club’s video analysis platform.

There should be a clear and consistent implementation of the playing style through each age, phase, and group. The playing style evidenced on match day should clearly reflect the club's P2 and P3 documents and should be unwavering regardless of result or match situation. Additionally, with reference to the 'Future Queensland Player' framework outlined in P2 and P3, the club should consistently bring to life the adopted playing style and methodology, ensuring a clear intention to support this framework through the club's unique playing style.

Players should consistently demonstrate the intent to execute the principles of the playing style throughout each key moment of the game. The readiness of the display may improve gradually from younger to older age groups. The focus is on the players' commitment and intent, rather than perfect execution of the principles, independent of the match result.

The maximum score for the Club Based Playing Style in planning may align with the potential maximum score for the team's adherence to the playing style. The rationale is that an underdeveloped playing style (focusing primarily on formation or basic team actions) is easier to implement than a well-developed framework, which allows players to gradually build their game knowledge. It is easily identifiable when clubs provide a high level of detail to their coaches and players, and when there is a strong club-wide understanding of the team model throughout the player development pathway.

It is beneficial if this collective effort and the development of the playing style are measured by the club’s Technical Directors and Technical Leads and shared with FQ to support the observation.

name: Individual Development and Player Behaviours (Match Day)
criteria:
No submission required. An observation of the club’s approach and conduct on match day focuses particularly on its players and their behaviours. Player behaviours are assessed in alignment with the club’s values, mission, vision and philosophy. This area also considers individual development and how it can and should be prioritized on match day. A high-performing club demonstrates clarity and consistency in outlining its approach, emphasizing individual player development over team results.

Individual development is central to the club's game-day delivery. This is evident in the coach’s ability to connect the game-day experience to the individual development plan (IDP) or focused learning objectives for each player. Individual targets may align with unit or team goals, but there is a clear understanding for each player regarding their specific focus for each game. While the outcome or state of the game may slightly influence a player’s tasks, the emphasis on individual focus remains consistent.

Player behaviours during the game are clearly linked to their assigned objectives or plans, whether set by the coach or self-determined. There is evidence of pre-planning with visual cues or targets, and the way this information is conveyed to players is clear and avoids unnecessary cognitive overload. Additionally, there is evidence of post-game or planned reviews—both objective and subjective—tied back to individual targets.

Players generally conduct themselves in the appropriate spirit of the game, demonstrating a commitment to a season-long development approach rather than focusing solely on winning a single match.

Full marks are awarded if there is clear consistency and alignment between the boys' and girls' programs in the delivery of the club's player development philosophy, coaching methodology, and delivery standards.

name: Coach Interaction Observation (Match Day)
criteria:
No submission required. Training observations are considered when assessing match day coaching to evaluate the transfer and consistency of learning outcomes, as well as the prioritization of long-term player development. The planning, preparation, conduct, and evaluation of match day activities are aligned with the club's vision, philosophy, and coaching methodology. Coaches are assessed on how their interactions reflect the club’s MVP and values, as outlined in their planning.

Assessment also examines whether match day planning is designed with specific technical or tactical objectives to meet individual and team needs. Effective organization is evidenced by timely execution, efficient use of warm-up time, appropriate allocation of field space and equipment, and optimal utilization of available staff. Coaches are evaluated on their ability to adapt and engage players through a variety of methods and technology before, during, and after the game. Interactions and feedback must be age- and stage-appropriate, encompassing team and individual tasks that are linked to learning outcomes.

The way coaches interact with players—including tone, body language, and timing—is also assessed. Coaches are expected to motivate, influence, and inspire players effectively. High scores are achieved through positive interactions with team members and club technical staff, fostering an exchange of ideas, knowledge sharing, and collaboration. Additionally, coaches are evaluated on their respectful and constructive interactions with officials, opposition staff, and players.

Match day evaluation involves engaging players and staff in reflective practices that analyse performance and learning outcomes. Finally, the appearance, behaviour, and overall conduct of the coach must consistently align with the club’s values and beliefs.

Full marks are awarded if there is clear consistency and alignment between the boys' and girls' programs in the delivery of the club's player development philosophy, coaching methodology, and delivery standards.

name: TD/TL Interaction Observation (Match Day)
criteria:
No submission required. The Technical Director (TD) and Technical Lead (TL) interaction observation on match day evaluates their conduct, management, and positive influence on the overall game-day experience. Together, they ensure that learning outcomes and adherence to the club’s values and Player Development Philosophy are maintained through their interactions with players, coaches, and staff.

The TD and/or TL are regularly present during game-day delivery across all phases of the club and serve as positive influences on coaches, players, and staff. They are instrumental in shaping coaching behaviours by providing timely and appropriate guidance aligned with the club’s expectations and playing methodology. Both roles actively support coaches and players throughout the day, contributing to pre-game, in-game, and post-game learning. This may include sitting on the bench with the coaching team to offer advice, providing feedback during breaks, or organising video recordings to ensure valuable learning moments are captured.

Following the game though not necessarily on match day the TD and/or TL conduct a formal debrief with staff, emphasising individual player development as the primary focus. This ensures that the developmental aspects of the game remain the key outcome of the day. Additionally, the TD and/or TL act as key points of communication and support for visiting referees and ground staff, fostering a supportive and professional environment.

The TD also plays a vital role in overseeing U18 games, ensuring a seamless transition within the club from the youth development phase to the performance phase. They maintain full awareness of all match-day operations, uphold the spirit of the game, demonstrate professional conduct, and ensure a positive and developmentally focused experience for everyone involved.

Full marks are awarded if there is clear consistency and alignment between the boys' and girls' programs in the resource allocation and delivery of the club's player development philosophy, coaching methodology, and delivery standards.

name: Players’ Self-Evaluations
criteria:
Prior to start of the season, players are educated on how to critically evaluate their own performance and complete structured self-assessments using the club’s designated platform. Initial evaluations are documented and used to establish individual development priorities, with clear performance targets and measurable outcomes agreed upon collaboratively between the player and technical staff. These discussions form the basis of each player's Individual Development Plan (IDP).

The club provides evidence that players complete regular self-assessment checkpoints to review progress, reflect on performance, adjust goals, and identify areas for continued improvement. Evaluations may be conducted through various methods, including face-to-face meetings, online forms, and video review sessions. Ideally, players are provided with match and training footage to support self-reflection and encourage meaningful dialogue with technical staff. All feedback, observations, and action points are recorded and referenced throughout the season to track development against agreed objectives.

Player self-assessments and IDP outcomes are reviewed as part of the club’s end-of-season evaluation process. The information gathered throughout the year provides a valuable foundation for coach, Technical Lead, and Technical Director reviews, supporting retention, progression, and future development planning. This comprehensive approach promotes player accountability, encourages continuous improvement, and reinforces a player-centred development environment.

name: Players’ Individual Development Plans
criteria:
The club maintains comprehensive and well-documented records of individual player feedback and assessments throughout the season. A structured Individual Development Plan (IDP) process is implemented using appropriate evaluation tools, delivery methods, timing, and follow-up procedures to ensure feedback is consistent, meaningful, and actionable. Players participate in a minimum of two formal reviews per season (ideally three), in addition to regular self-assessments.

The review process is closely aligned with the club’s goal-setting and IDP framework, providing regular checkpoints for players to reflect on progress, review development objectives, and measure performance against agreed goals. Feedback is tailored to each player’s technical, tactical, physical, and personal development needs, helping identify strengths, areas for improvement, and clear actions for future development.

Feedback incorporates input from age-group coaches, Technical Leads, the Technical Director, and other relevant staff where appropriate, providing a holistic view of player progress. Where age-appropriate, video analysis and objective performance data may be incorporated to support self-reflection and targeted development.

IDPs are regularly reviewed and refined to ensure development priorities remain relevant and aligned to each player’s needs and long-term objectives. Outcomes from player reviews, self-assessments, and IDPs inform player progression, retention, re-trial, release, and end-of-season decisions, with clear processes and outcomes communicated to players and parents.

name: Player Parent Education Events
evidence: Club visits, Supporting documents, Electronic Submission
criteria:
The club implements a planned schedule of player and parent workshops throughout the season, supplementing the yearly induction presentation. These educational events are incorporated into the academy’s annual plan and are accessible to all players across the club. The content and topics of the workshops are relevant and appropriately tailored to the ages and development stages of the participants. The material is presented in a clear and understandable manner for both players and parents, ensuring it facilitates future growth and learning.

Workshop sessions may cover a wide range of topics, including, but not limited to, the team model explanation, player evaluation procedures, match analysis, sport psychology, goal setting, injury prevention, nutrition, athlete wellbeing, and other relevant subjects. The workshops may feature leading industry experts to enhance the quality and depth of the content. Players are often encouraged to complete follow-up tasks to reinforce their learning, and online platforms may also be utilised to deliver workshop content for greater accessibility.

The club provides evidence of the workshops, including scheduled dates, attendee lists, workshop content, presentations (with clear date and location), and video recordings of the educational events. Additionally, in cases of wet weather or unforeseen circumstances, the club has alternative educational resources available, such as those hosted on the AIS website, FQ Hub, or the club’s own website.

A minimum of quarterly workshop delivery is expected in addition to the player induction presentation, ensuring consistent opportunities for education and development throughout the season.

name: Coaches’ Self-Evaluations
criteria:
The club demonstrates a strong commitment to informal education and collaboration for its academy coaching staff through the implementation of structured self-evaluation processes.

There is consistent and clear evidence of ongoing self-assessment across various activities, including video recording of training sessions, match review, pre-game team talks, half-time team talks, post-game team talks, club workshop delivery, and more (evidence should be dated).

The club strictly follows its review schedule and ensures that all self-assessments are documented using a dedicated form or template. Following these evaluations, coaches develop or review Individual Development Plans (IDPs), with multiple check-in points with the Technical Director/Technical Leads throughout the season to facilitate self-reflection and monitor progress.

name: Coaches' Individual Development Plans
criteria:
The club provides detailed evidence of the implementation of Individual Development Plans (IDPs) for all academy coaches. The club follows established processes for review frequency and documents evidence for all coaches, with check-in points scheduled throughout the season to track progress, at a minimum, on a quarterly basis (evidence should be dated).

Coaches are encouraged to focus on identified areas of strength and areas for improvement linked to personal and football competencies, with their IDPs set up to be appropriate for their stage of development. There is consistent evidence of IDPs showing a high level of detail, clear objectives, and ongoing reflection.

Coaches are given benchmarks and growth pathways for both personal and professional development and receive additional support, either internally or externally, through a mentor network, which includes, but is not limited to, Technical Directors, Technical Leads, Heads of Phase, senior coaches, experienced coaches, or peer mentoring between coaches.

There is a clear link between ongoing self-evaluation processes and the coaches’ IDPs, ensuring alignment between individual learning and club objectives. A season-ending performance review provides guidance to inform the next season’s plan. High coach retention may indicate that coaches are well-supported, valued, and cared for year after year.

name: Coach Mentoring
criteria:
The club provides detailed evidence of ongoing mentoring through both formal and informal coach development activities. The club demonstrates the implementation of a structured mentoring network for all Technical Leads, academy coaches and nominated Female Technical Lead, which includes the option to officially nominate a mentor for each coach. This network may include regular and ongoing access to industry experts, Technical Directors, Technical Leads, senior coaches, experienced coaches, coach developers, and peer mentors.

Regular mentoring sessions are structured with clear goals and specific outcomes, aligned with the club’s self-evaluation processes and each coach’s Individual Development Plan (IDP). These sessions are supported by feedback mechanisms, such as check-ins, written reflections, or observation reviews, that track progress over time.

There is clear evidence of documented goals and measurable outcomes achieved by academy coaches for continuous growth, with formal and informal mentoring monitored, recorded, and reviewed throughout the season.

Mentoring appears across multiple activities and contexts, including training and match reviews, workshops, peer observations, and inter-department collaboration. Confidentiality guidelines ensure a safe and respectful mentoring environment, fostering mutual benefits for both mentors and mentees, and contributing to a collaborative coaching culture across the club.

name: Coach Education Events
evidence: Club visits, Supporting documents, Electronic Submission
criteria:
The club plans and delivers a series of annual internal educational events to support coach education, aligning with its internal coach development strategy and each coach’s Individual Development Plan (IDP). These planned workshops and webinars are directly connected to the club’s player development philosophy and other topics of professional interest relevant to coaches from U9 to U18.

To maximise engagement and staff inclusion, training schedules include planned breaks for these events, ensuring participation without disrupting the program. Consideration is given to seasonal planning (e.g., Term 2 delivery or wet-weather rescheduling) to maintain consistency across the season. Educational events may also be delivered by other departments, such as sports science, physiotherapy, nutrition, or psychology. Staff are encouraged to have input into content design and delivery, taking on shared responsibility for shaping and presenting information that supports collective growth.

The club regularly invites external experts to lead specialist educational sessions, providing exposure to diverse perspectives and enriching the club’s learning culture. These workshops and webinars are also inclusive of wider partner clubs or schools, ensuring that the content delivered is relevant, practical, and impactful.

The outcomes and reflections from these events contribute to refining and improving the club’s practices and delivery methods. Video recordings, presentations, and supporting materials are made available to coaches and attendees following each event and are archived within the club’s permanent knowledge base for future access.

The club maintains an effective system for tracking attendance, documenting the date, time, location, presenters, staff in attendance, key themes, and session outcomes. Information about upcoming workshops is also shared in advance with FQ Club Development Ambassadors, offering them opportunities to attend and observe as part of the club’s transparent and developmental approach.

Coach and player/parent inductions are excluded from the scope of this requirement. Furthermore, workshop or education events delivered by FQ Staff or Club Ambassadors will not be considered, as they are delivered as part of the 2027 Club Development support process.

name: National Team Players (Socceroos/Matildas and Overseas)
criteria:
For this line item, submissions must only include players who have represented the Australian Senior National Team or an overseas Senior National Team in an official international fixture for their country. For overseas representatives, the national team must be ranked within the top 50 of the FIFA Women’s World Rankings or the top 100 of the FIFA Men’s World Rankings.

Clubs may include current or former players from the past seven years who have played at least two seasons for the club in an age-eligible junior or youth competition (U12–U18).

Players who represented the club more than seven years ago or who do not meet the above criteria must not be included.

To be awarded points for each eligible player, clubs MUST upload all relevant supporting evidence demonstrating compliance with the above criteria.

name: Professional Players (A-Leagues, Australian Championship & Overseas)
criteria:
For this line item, sumbission must only include full-time professional players (Women’s and Men’s). Players are only scored if they play in the top two tier leagues of countries ranked within the top 50 FIFA Women’s or top 100 FIFA Men’s.

Clubs may include players from the last five years who have played at least two seasons for the club in an age-eligible junior or youth competition (U12–U18). For Australia-based players, the A-League Men’s, A-League Women’s, and Australian Championships are accepted.

Players who represented the club more than five years ago or who do not meet the above criteria must not be included.

To be awarded points for each eligible player, clubs MUST upload all relevant supporting evidence demonstrating compliance with the above criteria.

name: Homegrown Players
criteria:
For this line item, submissions must only include Australian male or female players aged 23 years and under who have played and been registered with the club for a minimum of two seasons in an age-eligible junior or youth competition (U12-U18), and have played at least 30% of matches in the current season for the club's NPL, FQPL 1, or FQPL 2 Men's or Women's First Team.

Clubs may include players who satisfy the above eligibility criteria and are currently registered and competing within the club's First Team program. Players who have not completed a minimum of two seasons at the club within the eligible age groups, exceed the age limit, or do not meet the minimum match participation requirement must not be included.

To be awarded points for each eligible player, clubs MUST upload all relevant supporting evidence demonstrating compliance with the above criteria.

name: National Youth Team Players (Young Socceroos/Joeys and Young/Junior Matildas and overseas)
criteria:
For this line item, submission must only include Australian players who have represented a Football Australia National Youth Team, as well as overseas players who have represented their country in an official international fixture. Clubs may also include players who have represented an overseas national team ranked within the top 50 of the FIFA Women's World Rankings or the top 100 of the FIFA Men's World Rankings.

Clubs may include current or former players from the last five years who have played a minimum of one season for the club in an age-eligible junior or youth competition (U12-U18). Players who represented the club more than five years ago or who do not meet the above eligibility criteria must not be included.

To be awarded points for each eligible player, clubs MUST upload all relevant supporting evidence demonstrating compliance with the above criteria.

name: Full-Time Queensland State Team Players
criteria:
For this line item, players selected and signed to the full-time Queensland State Team (QST) programs will be considered. This includes both male and female players progressing from club-based programs to the full-time QST programs during the current Club Development & Assessment year.

Clubs will be recognised by Football Queensland for their contribution to the development of these players, provided the player has been registered with and developed at the club within the past three seasons.

No submission is required from clubs for Queensland-based players, as FQ will assess eligibility following the QST program selection process.

name: Club Based Queensland State Team Players
criteria:
For this line item, Club-Based State Team players are those selected to represent the Member Federation Boys’ or Girls’ State Teams during the current Club Development & Assessment year. School representative programs and non-FA-affiliated futsal representation will not be considered.

FQ Academy clubs will also be recognised by Football Queensland for their contribution to the development of selected State Team players, provided the player has been registered with and developed at the club within the past three seasons.

No submission is required for Queensland-based players, as FQ will assess eligibility following the State Team selection process.

name: Talented Player Programs (FQ Emerging & FQ Academy Regional Programs)
criteria:
For this line item, Talented Support Program players are those aged U13–U16 who have been officially selected into an FQ Emerging (Metro) or FQ Academy Regional program during the current Club Development & Assessment year, but have not been selected to represent an outdoor State Team.

No submission is required for Queensland-based players, as FQ will assess eligibility following the relevant program selection process.

name: Progressing Players
criteria: This area of assessment is designed to indicate how effectively identified players are supported to progress through the FA/FQ player development pyramid.  The club should provide evidence for moving players through this pathway.  The club is in regular discussion with a prospective new club and may even have a formal agreement in place, that might lead to trials in season (with the current club's consent).  Player losses/movement are pre-planned to help avoid mass open trials. To score highly in this area there must be evidence that at least 1 player has progressed the player pathway with the level of communication and transparency as detailed above. Players that move to another club at the end of the season do not simply leave the club as they want to play in a different environment. Scoring in this area is applicable to Silver, Bronze and Development Committed rated clubs only.

name: Talent Identification Database & Management
criteria:
Football Queensland and Football Australia are committed to building a comprehensive Talent ID database.

For Pool A clubs, a collaborative approach through player recommendations for QST selection, active communication with FQ’s Talent ID network, and the consistent submission of Talent ID forms at FQ Academy fixtures, TDS, and Carnivals will directly influence scoring outcomes.

For Pool B and C clubs, positive attendance and support at Talent ID events and Carnivals, along with the timely submission of Talent ID forms, are key evidence points for strong performance in this criterion.

All Technical Directors are expected to attend Talent ID workshops, contribute to player identification, and maintain regular Talent ID submissions. A full-year calendar outlining key age-specific data collection points will be provided to clubs to support this process.

name: Player Retention
criteria:
Clubs are required to complete the provided 'O10 – Player Retention' template for the u9-u18 teams as part of the non-negotiables (item NN4), located in the club folder in the FQ Club Development Hub. Player retention is calculated for academy players for the u10-u18 teams. Any players who departed the club due to progressing to a higher ranked club are classified as 'retained players' and are required to be listed in the appropriate section of the template. Evidence between clubs must be provided for any player passed on to a higher ranked club.

In regional areas, the assessment focus is further expanded to include internal player progression into the club’s senior QPL environment, or supporting players who leave the region to pursue education, training, or advanced football opportunities.

The player retention scoring breakdown is as follows:

• Percentage >= 85% = 3 points

• 80% =< percentage < 85% = 2.7 points

• 75% =< percentage < 80% = 2.4 points

• 70% =< percentage < 75% = 2.1 points

• 65% =< percentage < 70% = 1.8 points

• 60% =< percentage < 65% = 1.5 points

• 55% =< percentage < 60% = 1.2 points

• 50% =< percentage < 55% = 0.9 points

• Percentage < 50% = 0 points

name: Coach Retention
criteria:
Coach retention information will be collected through the Technical Staff Qualification submission via the template located in the club's folder in the FQ Club Development Hub.

Coach retention is calculated based on the technical staff (Technical Director, Technical leads and Head Coaches) being retained from the previous year, recognising the club's ability to retain staff and provide continuity within its technical development program. Additional points will be awarded for staff who have been at the club for at least three years, with a higher weighting applied to the Technical Director (TD) and Technical Leads.

Coaches progressing from the club's community football programs into its academy program, or from an assistant role to a head coach role will be considered retained coaches.

Similarly to O10 - Player Retention, coaches progressing to higher-ranked clubs will also be recognised as retained, provided there is evidence of a prior agreement between the two clubs supporting the coach's progression.

The coach retention scoring breakdown is as follows:

• Percentage >= 85% = 3 points

• 80% =< percentage < 85% = 2.7 points

• 75% =< percentage < 80% = 2.4 points

• 70% =< percentage < 75% = 2.1 points

• 65% =< percentage < 70% = 1.8 points

• 60% =< percentage < 65% = 1.5 points

• 55% =< percentage < 60% = 1.2 points

• 50% =< percentage < 55% = 0.9 points

• Percentage < 50% = 0 points

name: Member Experience Surveys
criteria:
A survey will be distributed twice by FQ to parents of u9-u18 registered players of your club. FQ will also ask the clubs to distribute the survey link to their members.

The first collection point will take place in March/April, focusing on club onboarding and early satisfaction with the player development program. The second collection point will occur at the end of August, gathering overall feedback from the season. An average Net Promoter Score (NPS) will be calculated across both data points to form each club’s final score.
